kf1.tip: Pick the odd one out of the sensory register, short-term memory and long-term memory, first by capacity, then by duration, and say why each time.
kf1.note: By capacity, most pick short-term memory as the odd one out. It holds only about 7 items, while the other two are large or potentially unlimited. By duration, a strong answer could pick the sensory register, which lasts only fractions of a second. It could also pick long-term memory, the only store that can be permanent. Either works if you explain it. If you said the sensory register has a small capacity, you mixed up how brief it is with how much it holds.

kf2.tip: Pick a phone number you know by heart and one you saw only once. Use acoustic and semantic coding and STM's 7 ±2 limit to explain why only one stuck.
kf2.note: A good answer follows both numbers through the stores. The number you saw once was held in STM, coded acoustically as sounds in your head. STM holds only about 7 items, plus or minus 2. Without rehearsal it fades within about 30 seconds, so that number was lost. You repeated the number you know many times. That rehearsal moved it into LTM, where it is coded semantically, by meaning. If you leave out rehearsal as the bridge between STM and LTM, you miss the key step.

cs1.tip: Imagine Peterson & Peterson's participants had not counted backwards in threes. Say how recall of the trigram at 18 seconds would change from about 5%, and why.
cs1.note: Most would say recall at 18 seconds would be much higher than about 5%. Counting backwards was there to stop rehearsal. Without it, participants could repeat the trigram and keep it active in STM. A strong answer adds that the study would then no longer measure STM duration without rehearsal, which was its aim. The trap is to say STM itself would last longer. In fact the trigram would simply be refreshed by rehearsal.
